doc.title: Chico Hamilton interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 30, 2000

title: Technology in recording and the sound of the drum
summary: Technology is fine but needs good hands; engineers destroyed natural drum sound.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Do you think technology has been a positive influence on recording or not?

Technology is dynamite. I’m all for it. But it’s the people, it’s the hands that are behind, that are controlling the technology. I think they should grow as well as the technical aspects of technology. Does that make sense?

You know? I think the hands — you know it’s just like there is no substitute for breath blowing instrument. You can put your hand on a key and hold that note for two weeks if you want to. But you can’t hold a note breathing for two weeks. So holding that note, breathing that breath when you do decide to breathe, it comes under the heading of phrasing. And what that phrasing is all about is what your heart, your head, your ears, your soul feels and hears. Not how long that sustaining power is, you know?
Yeah. It’s like that bass player who played your melody.
You can breathe with that thing and see it.
So the technology of the technicians is fantastic but the technicians themselves should become as contemporary as the instruments that they are playing with. Does that make sense?

Because it’s just like a God damn engineer man, destroyed the drum in the studio, they destroyed the natural sound of the drum. They’ve got it so padded, they’ve got it this — the drum doesn’t sound like a drum anymore. It doesn’t sound like — whoever’s playing, you don’t hear their sound. They all sound alike [scats].
